name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Monday 14 July 1986

clue.text: Make a lot of noise around 'ere and below it

indicators.note: one word is wrapped around the other, which sits inside it

blocks.note: to thunder is to make a loud booming noise
taken as written, with the dropped aitch restored as a different word meaning before

explanation.surface: A cockney shouting round here and underneath.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe makes ''ere' look like dropped-H 'here'; it is just the letters ERE.
explanation.definitionFit: Thereunder is a formal or legal adverb meaning beneath that, or under the thing just mentioned.

clue.text: Loose ropes encircling round of race-course slip out of place

indicators.note: something loose is not held in its set arrangement, so the letters are rearranged
to encircle is to surround, putting one word inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
one circuit of a track is a lap

explanation.surface: Loose ropes around a racetrack make a runner trip and fall.
explanation.definitionFit: In medicine, an organ that prolapses slips down from its normal position in the body.

clue.text: See the man at the wheel dawdle

blocks.note: first meaning: a craftsman who throws clay on a wheel
second meaning: to move about in an aimless, unhurried way

explanation.surface: Watch the driver, who is going painfully slowly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The man at the wheel' suggests a driver or helmsman; the wheel is a ceramicist's.
explanation.definitionFit: A maker of ceramics works at a spinning wheel, and to potter about means to dither idly.

clue.text: King tucking into tender chicken?

indicators.note: something tucked into another thing ends up inside it

blocks.note: to tender is to make an offer or bid
R stands for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A monarch eating a nice soft piece of chicken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tender chicken' reads as a description of the meat; tender is a verb meaning offer.
explanation.definitionFit: A chicken is one example of a feathered creature, which the question mark flags as a definition by example.

clue.text: Initially woman, quite feminine, gets let down: she's not invited to dance

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word it goes with

blocks.note: the first letter of the word
quite, as in 'all alone', meaning entirely
F is the abbreviation for feminine
to lower something is to let it down

explanation.surface: A very feminine woman is disappointed at being left out of the dancing.
explanation.definitionFit: A wallflower is someone left sitting at the side of a dance because nobody asks them, an idiom from flowers growing on walls.

clue.text: A window, one fitted in a series of steps

indicators.note: something fitted in goes inside the thing that receives it

blocks.note: a flight of stairs
an is the indefinite article meaning one

explanation.surface: A builder fitting a window halfway up a staircase.
explanation.definitionFit: A fanlight is a semicircular pane set above a door, often with radiating bars like a fan.

clue.text: Slander shows abysmal ignorance, to some extent

indicators.note: only some of the words are used, a stretch running across them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: Defamation reveals how badly ignorant the speaker is.
explanation.definitionFit: To malign someone is to speak ill of them falsely, which is what slander means as a verb.

clue.text: A bullet that travels very slowly

blocks.note: first meaning: a lump of metal fired from a gun
second meaning: a shell-less garden mollusc, a byword for slowness

explanation.walkthrough: Bullets are the fastest things around, so a slow one sounds absurd; the second half describes a different creature with the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: Slug is slang for a bullet, and it is also the slimy creature that creeps along gardens at a crawl.

clue.text: On a march I blow a musical instrument

indicators.note: as in 'blow it all about': letters that are blown scatter and land in a new order

blocks.note: nine letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A marching bandsman admits to playing a mouth organ as they step along.
explanation.definitionFit: A harmonica, or mouth organ, is a small reed instrument played by breathing in and out across it.

clue.text: To be of use, you need a disguise, by the sound of it

indicators.note: says we want what the phrase sounds like when spoken, not how it is written

blocks.note: a veil hides the face, so it serves as a disguise

explanation.surface: Advice to a spy: if you want to be useful, go in disguise.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'a veil' quickly and it is indistinguishable from the verb meaning to help.
explanation.definitionFit: To avail is to be of benefit or help, as in 'it will avail you nothing'.

clue.text: Kin, out of office, blushing about it

indicators.note: one word goes round the other, surrounding it on both sides

blocks.note: red in the face from embarrassment
'the late chairman' means the former one, no longer in post

explanation.surface: A relative who has lost their job is red-faced about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'it' points back to being out of office, so that phrase is what the red goes round.
explanation.definitionFit: People who are kin are related to each other by blood or marriage; the adjective swaps for the noun used predicatively.

clue.text: Yearn to hold bad back, sprawling about

indicators.note: going back means the word is read from its end to its start
holding something means keeping it inside, so one word sits within the other

blocks.note: to long for something is to yearn for it
ill as in 'ill will', meaning bad

explanation.surface: Someone pining with a bad back is sprawled about on the sofa.
explanation.definitionFit: To loll is to lounge or lie lazily, so lolling about is sprawling in a relaxed way.

clue.text: Superior meal, but without an entree

indicators.note: the entree is the way in, so the meal loses the letter it opens with

blocks.note: an evening meal

explanation.surface: A fine dinner that somehow skips the starter course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entree' looks like a dinner course, but here it means entrance: the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Upper means higher in rank or position, as in the upper classes, so it is a synonym for superior.

clue.text: A coach for French, and what one expects of his pupils?

definitions.text: what one expects of his pupils

blocks.note: first meaning: a French public stagecoach

blocks.clueFragment: what one expects of his pupils
blocks.note: second meaning: hard, careful work

explanation.surface: A French tutor and the effort a teacher demands from a class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coach' reads as a tutor of French; it is a horse-drawn vehicle used in France.
explanation.definitionFit: The French stagecoach was called a diligence, and the same word means steady, conscientious effort expected of a student.

clue.text: Get ratty with a camel?

blocks.note: first meaning: behave like rats, which are said to abandon a sinking vessel
second meaning: the animal known as the ship of the desert

explanation.surface: Losing your temper with an awkward camel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ratty' usually means irritable; here it means acting like a rat leaving a vessel. Read the other way, the phrase names the camel.
explanation.definitionFit: The camel is proverbially the ship of the desert, and to quit a vessel in trouble is what rats famously do.

clue.text: Damage he got in the heel in final part of course

indicators.note: damaged letters are knocked out of their order and must be rebuilt

blocks.note: fourteen letters taken as written

explanation.surface: An Achilles-style injury picked up near the finish of a race.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a running course; the answer is a golf course.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard round of golf has eighteen holes, so the last one played finishes the course.

clue.text: Behaves characteristically, when I do this song in variety

indicators.note: variety means a mixed assortment, so the letters come out in a different mix

blocks.note: fifteen letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A music-hall singer says their signature number in a variety show is true to type.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Variety' suggests the music-hall stage, but it is the signal to mix the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To do one's own thing is an idiom for acting as one naturally would, following personal inclination.

clue.text: Driven forward, he had, gripping a machine-gun

indicators.note: what is gripped is held inside the grasp

blocks.note: he'd is the contraction of he had, apostrophe dropped
taken as written
the Sten was a British submachine gun of the Second World War

explanation.surface: A soldier charges ahead clutching his machine-gun.
explanation.definitionFit: To hasten is to hurry or speed something along, so hastened means urged or pushed on quickly.

clue.text: At home I'm in charge also, not so unfriendly

indicators.note: says the word that comes before loses these two letters

blocks.note: to be in means to be at home
taken as written, apostrophe dropped
IC is the standard abbreviation for in charge
taken as written

explanation.surface: A host says they are the boss at home too, and not quite so hostile now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not so unfriendly' reads as a comparative, but 'not so' acts on the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Inimical means hostile or harmful, from the Latin for enemy, so it is a formal synonym.

clue.text: Recorder gets point right in middle of back

indicators.note: placing something in the middle of a word means it goes inside, splitting that word

blocks.note: the back of something is its rear
the gist of an argument is its main point
R is the usual abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A recorder player picks up a tip about the centre of the back, like a music lesson on posture.
explanation.definitionFit: A registrar is the official who records births, marriages and deaths, so a keeper of records.

clue.text: Go over undulating track

indicators.note: undulating means moving in waves, so the letters are shifted about

blocks.note: six letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A walker crosses a hilly path.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go over' looks like the definition of a verb; it is the raw letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A groove is a channel or rut, like the track cut in a record that a needle follows.

clue.text: A drink of beer when eating duck produces a tip

indicators.note: what is eaten ends up inside the eater, so one word goes into the other

blocks.note: a pint is a standard serving of beer
a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, written as a zero

explanation.surface: Having a beer while eating roast duck gives one a helpful suggestion.
explanation.definitionFit: The point of a pencil or a spear is its sharp end, so point and tip are synonyms.

clue.text: Walk beyond the narrow defile before the lad loses heart

indicators.note: one part is placed ahead of the next, fixing the order they are joined in
the heart of a word is its central letter, which is removed

blocks.note: a narrow route through mountains
a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: A hiker goes on past a mountain gorge ahead of a disheartened youngster.
explanation.definitionFit: To pass by something is to go past it without stopping, the same as walking beyond it.

clue.text: Sequence of operations revealed by retiring CO among journalists

indicators.note: retiring means withdrawing or going back, so the letters run the other way
being among a group means being surrounded by it

blocks.note: journalists collectively are the press
taken as written; CO is a commanding officer

explanation.surface: Reporters uncover the routine by which a commanding officer leaves the army.
explanation.definitionFit: A process is a series of actions or steps carried out to achieve a result.

clue.text: The wine that's left

blocks.note: first meaning: a fortified wine from Portugal
second meaning: the left-hand side of a ship

explanation.surface: The wine that remains after the party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' reads as 'remaining'; it is the nautical direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Port is a sweet fortified wine, and on a ship port is the side to the left when facing forward.

clue.text: There's entertainment here — I say! — and some hot stuff

blocks.note: ho is an exclamation used to call attention, like 'I say!'
spice is what makes food hot

explanation.surface: A showman announces a venue with a hot act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entertainment' here is the old sense of hospitality to guests, which a hospice was built to give travellers.
explanation.definitionFit: A hospice was originally a lodging run by monks offering hospitality to travellers and pilgrims, a place of entertainment in the old sense.

clue.text: See 15
Show regret about evening being cut short

indicators.note: cutting something short trims off its final letter
one word goes round another, enclosing it

blocks.note: to rue is to regret
eve is a poetic word for evening

explanation.surface: Someone expresses sorrow that their evening ended early.
explanation.definitionFit: A revue is a theatrical show of sketches, songs and dances, often topical.

clue.text: Vain expression of pride, having lazy Sunday in sailing vessel

indicators.note: one part sits inside the other, enclosed by it

blocks.note: idle means lazy
a boat is a vessel
S is a standard abbreviation for Sunday

explanation.surface: A yachtsman brags about a lazy Sunday spent on board.
explanation.definitionFit: An idle boast is an empty brag, with no substance behind the pride it claims.
